summary: Defines the syntaxes used by LDAPv3 for attribute values and the rules for writing those values as octet strings during transmission. It was replaced by RFCs 4510, 4512, 4517 and 4523.

eli5.summary: It lists the kinds of facts a directory stores, like text or numbers, and how each is written when sent.

questions: how are ldap attribute values encoded
what is an ldap attribute syntax
how is a directory string encoded in ldap
subtitle: How LDAPv3 describes the kinds of values a directory can hold and writes each one as plain octets.

tldr.problem: LDAP carries attribute values as octet strings, so clients and servers need agreed rules for what each kind of value looks like and how it is written.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a set of syntaxes named by object identifiers, with a string encoding for each, plus the notation for describing attribute types, object classes and matching rules. It also lists the attributes, object classes and matching rules servers should support.
tldr.outcome: This Proposed Standard was replaced by RFC 4510, RFC 4512, RFC 4517 and RFC 4523, and updated by RFC 3377.

today: RFC 2252 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 4510, RFC 4512, RFC 4517 and RFC 4523. It was also updated by RFC 3377.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) requires that the contents of AttributeValue fields be octet strings. This document defines a set of syntaxes for LDAPv3 and the rules for representing values of those syntaxes as octet strings. Other documents that define attribute types refer to these syntaxes.

The overview calls the document a framework for building schemas. A schema is the collection of attribute type definitions, object class definitions and other information a server uses to decide how to match a filter or compare assertion against an entry, and whether to allow add and modify operations.

An IESG note warns that update access needs secure authentication, which the document does not mandate. Until a mandatory authentication mechanism is standardized, clients and servers using update functions are unlikely to interoperate, and implementors are discouraged from deploying update functionality.
sections.eli5: Computers can only send plain strings of bytes, so they need rules for turning each kind of fact into bytes and back again.

sections.title: Describing Attributes, Classes and Matching Rules
sections.content:
Schema elements are written as parenthesized strings that begin with an object identifier, followed by optional keywords. An attribute type description can include NAME, DESC, SUP, EQUALITY, ORDERING, SUBSTR, SYNTAX, SINGLE-VALUE, NO-USER-MODIFICATION and USAGE. Names beginning with X- are reserved for private experiments.

An object class is abstract, structural or auxiliary, with MUST and MAY lists of attributes. Every entry contains an abstract class (top or alias), at least one structural class, and zero or more auxiliary classes. A matching rule tells a server how to compare attribute values with assertion values in Search and Compare operations.

Servers that recognize extra attributes, classes or matching rules MUST publish their definitions in the subschema entry. Schema developers MUST NOT create names that conflict with those in existing standards-track RFCs.
sections.eli5: Each kind of fact in the address book gets a short definition card: its name, what kind of thing it holds, and how to tell whether two of them match.

sections.title: Syntaxes and Their Encodings
sections.content:
Each syntax is named by a dotted-decimal object identifier under 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1. For example, Directory String is 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.15 and Generalized Time is ...121.1.24. A suggested maximum length may be added in braces, as in {64}. The document strongly deprecates defining new arbitrary syntaxes because it hurts interoperability, and says most attributes should use the Directory String syntax.

Encodings are mostly plain text. Directory String is UTF-8, Boolean is TRUE or FALSE, INTEGER is the decimal digits, and Generalized Time looks like 199412161032Z with GMT strongly recommended. A Postal Address joins lines with $, and a DN uses the string form from RFC 2253. Where a separator must appear inside a string, a backslash followed by two hexadecimal digits is used.

Some values have no string form. Certificates and certificate lists MUST only be transferred with the binary encoding, by requesting attributes such as userCertificate;binary. Clients MUST NOT assume an unrecognized syntax is a string.
sections.eli5: Each kind of fact has its own spelling rule: words are written as words, numbers as digits, and things like pictures are sent as raw bytes instead.

sections.title: Standard Attributes, Classes and Matching Rules
sections.content:
Servers MUST recognize the attribute types in sections 5.1 to 5.3. These include operational attributes such as createTimestamp, modifyTimestamp, creatorsName, modifiersName and subschemaSubentry, and the subschema attributes attributeTypes, objectClasses, matchingRules and matchingRuleUse.

A second group lives only in the root DSE: namingContexts, altServer, supportedExtension, supportedControl, supportedSASLMechanisms and supportedLDAPVersion. They let a client discover what a server masters and supports. A client can use namingContexts to choose suitable search base objects.

The document also defines the optional extensibleObject class, which lets an entry hold any attribute, and the subschema class. Servers that support the extensible match filter SHOULD offer matching rules such as caseIgnoreMatch, integerMatch, generalizedTimeMatch and caseIgnoreSubstringsMatch.
sections.eli5: The note also lists a starter set of cards every directory must know, including ones that tell visitors what the directory itself can do.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC raises two points. First, directory attributes describe real-world people, organizations and devices, and most countries have privacy laws about publishing information about people.

Second, turning a value from its X.501 form into an LDAP string is not always reversible to the same BER or DER form. For example, a distinguished name with CN=Sam looks identical whether the value was a TeletexString or a PrintableString. Applications that must rebuild the DER form, such as when verifying an X.509 certificate, SHOULD NOT use the string representation and SHOULD use the Binary syntax instead.
sections.eli5: Address books can hold private facts about people, so be careful who sees them. Also, a written-down copy can lose small details, so use the exact original when checking an ID.
